<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priors
<br class="ltx_break">for Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ibne Farabi Shihab
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sanjeda Akter
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Anuj Sharma
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:Equal%20contribution."><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{ishihab, sanjeda, anujs}@iastate.edu<sup id="id1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">*</span></sup></span>Equal contribution.</a>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Civil, Construction and Environmental Engineering, Iowa State University
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Computer Science, Iowa State University
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA enable practical adaptation of large language models but provide no principled uncertainty estimates, leading to poorly calibrated predictions and unreliable behavior under domain shift. We introduce Stiefel-Bayes Adapters (SBA), a Bayesian PEFT framework that places a Matrix Langevin prior over orthonormal adapter factors on the Stiefel manifold <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> and performs approximate posterior inference via tangent space Laplace approximation with geodesic retraction. Unlike Gaussian priors in flat space projected onto orthogonality constraints, our prior on the manifold naturally encodes the inductive bias that adapter subspaces should be well conditioned and orthogonal, while the posterior provides calibrated predictive uncertainty without recalibration. We prove formally that the tangent space approximation strictly avoids the structural variance inflation inherent in projecting from ambient space, establishing a rigorous theoretical advantage for intrinsic manifold inference. Across GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks on RoBERTa-large, LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-13B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B, domain shift evaluations, selective prediction protocols, and an abstractive summarization task, SBA achieves task performance comparable to LoRA and DoRA while reducing Expected Calibration Error by 18 to 34% over deterministic baselines, improving selective prediction AUROC by 12 to 25% under domain shift, and outperforming deep ensembles of five LoRA models on OOD detection at a fraction of the parameter cost. Our results demonstrate that where you place uncertainty, on the right geometric structure, matters more than simply adding any Bayesian treatment to adapters.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models adapted via parameter-efficient fine-tuning have become the standard paradigm for task-specific deployment. Methods such as LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, DoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and orthogonal adaptations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> achieve competitive performance while updating only a fraction of model parameters. However, these methods produce point estimates of adapter weights, yielding no principled uncertainty quantification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This gap has serious practical consequences. Deployed NLP systems must know when they are likely wrong: clinical NLP models should abstain rather than hallucinate diagnoses, and legal document classifiers should flag uncertain predictions for human review. Recent work has shown that LLMs are frequently overconfident <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadavath et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiong and others, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and others, 2023</a>)</cite>, and that this miscalibration worsens after preference alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao and others, 2025</a>)</cite>, making reliable uncertainty estimation an increasingly urgent problem. Current PEFT methods cannot do this reliably. Post-hoc calibration techniques such as temperature scaling partially address calibration on in-distribution data, but they degrade under domain shift <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li and others, 2023</a>)</cite>—precisely the setting where reliable uncertainty is most needed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A natural remedy is Bayesian inference over adapter parameters. Prior work has explored Gaussian priors over LoRA weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and MC-Dropout applied to adapter layers. These approaches treat the adapter weight space as flat Euclidean space, ignoring the geometric structure that successful adapters implicitly exploit: the most effective adapters learn low-rank, well-conditioned subspace transformations that correspond to points on or near the Stiefel manifold of orthonormal frames. Recent work has confirmed this empirically: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al. (2025)</a></cite> show that optimizing LoRA’s <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> matrix on the Stiefel manifold achieves near-perfect orthogonality and full effective rank, dramatically improving parameter efficiency, demonstrating that the Stiefel geometry is not merely a theoretical convenience but a practically important structural property of adapter subspaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We argue that geometry-aware Bayesian inference over adapters yields fundamentally better uncertainty estimates than geometry-agnostic alternatives. By placing a Matrix Langevin distribution as a prior directly on the Stiefel manifold <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>, we obtain a prior that naturally regularizes adapter factors toward orthonormality without hard constraints, a posterior whose concentration reflects genuine epistemic uncertainty about the adapter subspace, and predictive distributions that are well calibrated without post-hoc adjustments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our work makes four contributions. First, we introduce Stiefel-Bayes Adapters (SBA), the first PEFT method with a geometry-aware Bayesian prior on the Stiefel manifold for LLM fine-tuning. Second, we develop a scalable inference procedure combining tangent space Laplace approximation with geodesic retraction, adding fewer than 8% wall-clock overhead over deterministic LoRA, and we prove formally that this geometry-aware approximation completely avoids the systematic variance inflation of the flat-space alternative (Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Geometric Variance Inflation &amp; KL Tightness). ‣ 4 Why Geometry Matters: Formal Analysis ‣ Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priorsfor Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Third, we provide comprehensive reliability evaluation across calibration, selective prediction, and OOD detection on five models spanning four architecture families, under both in-distribution and domain shift settings, including a generative summarization task. Fourth, we demonstrate that manifold-aware priors systematically outperform flat-space Bayesian baselines and even deep ensembles of LoRA models, establishing that geometric structure in the prior is the key ingredient for adapter uncertainty.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We review the three building blocks of our approach: parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the Stiefel manifold, and the Matrix Langevin distribution. These concepts converge naturally in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Method: Stiefel-Bayes Adapters ‣ Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priorsfor Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, where we construct the SBA framework.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a pretrained weight matrix <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>, LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=W_{0}+BA" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=W_{0}+BA</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\ll d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\ll d</annotation></semantics></math> is the adapter rank. The effective update therefore lies in a rank-<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> subspace. Orthogonal variants constrain <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> (or both factors) to have orthonormal columns, i.e., <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})=\{U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}:U^{\top}U=I_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})=\{U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}:U^{\top}U=I_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Stiefel manifold. This improves conditioning and training stability but remains a point estimate, providing no uncertainty quantification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>The Stiefel Manifold</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Stiefel manifold <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> is the set of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\times k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\times k</annotation></semantics></math> matrices with orthonormal columns. It is a compact Riemannian submanifold of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}</annotation></semantics></math> with dimension <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dk-k(k+1)/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dk-k(k+1)/2</annotation></semantics></math>. The tangent space at <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U\in\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U\in\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{U}\mathrm{St}(k,d)=\{\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}:U^{\top}\Delta+\Delta^{\top}U=0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>U</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>St</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{U}\mathrm{St}(k,d)=\{\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}:U^{\top}\Delta+\Delta^{\top}U=0\}</annotation></semantics></math>. To map tangent vectors back to the manifold, we use the QR-based geodesic retraction <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Retr}_{U}(\Delta)=\mathrm{qf}(U+\Delta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Retr</mi><mi>U</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>qf</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Retr}_{U}(\Delta)=\mathrm{qf}(U+\Delta)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{qf}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>qf</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{qf}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the Q-factor of a QR decomposition.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The compactness of <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> is important for our purposes: it means that the Matrix Langevin distribution is always normalizable (unlike Gaussian distributions on unbounded spaces, which require careful handling of improper priors). The dimension formula <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dk-k(k+1)/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dk-k(k+1)/2</annotation></semantics></math> shows that the manifold has fewer degrees of freedom than the ambient space <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}</annotation></semantics></math>, with the deficit <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k(k+1)/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k(k+1)/2</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to the orthonormality constraints. For typical adapter dimensions (<math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=4096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4096</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=4096</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=16</annotation></semantics></math>), the manifold dimension is 65,400 compared to the ambient dimension of 65,536, so the constraint removes only 136 dimensions—a small fraction, but one that has outsized impact on the posterior geometry as we show in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Why Geometry Matters: Formal Analysis ‣ Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priorsfor Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>The Matrix Langevin Distribution</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Matrix Langevin distribution on <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> has density <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chikuse, 2003</a>)</cite></p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(U\mid F)=\frac{1}{{}_{0}F_{1}(\tfrac{d}{2};\tfrac{1}{4}F^{\top}F)}\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(F^{\top}U)\big)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>U</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>F</mi><mprescripts></mprescripts><mn>1</mn><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn><mrow></mrow></mmultiscripts><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(U\mid F)=\frac{1}{{}_{0}F_{1}(\tfrac{d}{2};\tfrac{1}{4}F^{\top}F)}\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(F^{\top}U)\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}</annotation></semantics></math> is the parameter matrix and <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{0}F_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mmultiscripts><mi>F</mi><mprescripts></mprescripts><mn>1</mn><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn><mrow></mrow></mmultiscripts><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{0}F_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is the hypergeometric function of matrix argument. The mode of this distribution is <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}=\mathrm{polar}(F)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>polar</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}=\mathrm{polar}(F)</annotation></semantics></math>, the closest orthonormal matrix to <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> obtained via polar decomposition <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=U^{*}S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=U^{*}S</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> positive semidefinite. The singular values of <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> control concentration: larger singular values yield a distribution more concentrated around <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. This makes the Matrix Langevin an ideal prior for adapter factors, since <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> encodes both the preferred adapter direction (via its polar factor) and our prior confidence (via its singular values).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To build intuition, consider the limiting cases. When <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=0</annotation></semantics></math>, the Matrix Langevin reduces to the uniform (Haar) distribution on <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>, expressing complete ignorance about the adapter subspace. When <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|F\|\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|F\|\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, the distribution concentrates on a single point <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}=\mathrm{polar}(F)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>polar</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}=\mathrm{polar}(F)</annotation></semantics></math>, recovering a deterministic adapter. Between these extremes, the singular values of <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> interpolate smoothly between ignorance and certainty, providing a natural scale for prior confidence that has no analogue in flat-space Gaussian priors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The normalizing constant <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{0}F_{1}(\tfrac{d}{2};\tfrac{1}{4}F^{\top}F)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>F</mi><mprescripts></mprescripts><mn>1</mn><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn><mrow></mrow></mmultiscripts><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{0}F_{1}(\tfrac{d}{2};\tfrac{1}{4}F^{\top}F)</annotation></semantics></math> is a hypergeometric function of matrix argument that does not have a closed form. We use the saddle-point approximation of Kume and Wood, which is accurate to <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(d^{-2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(d^{-2})</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\geq 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\geq 32</annotation></semantics></math>. We validate this approximation empirically in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Normalizer Approximation Validation ‣ Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priorsfor Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method: Stiefel-Bayes Adapters</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now describe the SBA framework (illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.2 Tangent Space Laplace Approximation ‣ 3 Method: Stiefel-Bayes Adapters ‣ Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priorsfor Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>): the probabilistic model, the inference procedure, and the computational overhead.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Model Specification</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each adapted layer <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>, we parameterize the low-rank update as</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta W^{(\ell)}=U^{(\ell)}\Sigma^{(\ell)}V^{(\ell)\top}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em">⊤</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta W^{(\ell)}=U^{(\ell)}\Sigma^{(\ell)}V^{(\ell)\top}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{(\ell)}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{(\ell)}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{(\ell)}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{(\ell)}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}})</annotation></semantics></math> are orthonormal factors on Stiefel manifolds, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>diag</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k})</annotation></semantics></math> contains learnable singular values in <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math>. We place independent Matrix Langevin priors on each orthonormal factor,</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle U^{(\ell)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle U^{(\ell)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{ML}(F_{U}^{(\ell)}),\quad V^{(\ell)}\sim\mathrm{ML}(F_{V}^{(\ell)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>ML</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>ML</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{ML}(F_{U}^{(\ell)}),\quad V^{(\ell)}\sim\mathrm{ML}(F_{V}^{(\ell)})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">and a Gaussian prior on the singular values <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>. The prior parameters are set via <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=\kappa_{0}\cdot U_{\mathrm{init}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>init</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=\kappa_{0}\cdot U_{\mathrm{init}}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{\mathrm{init}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>init</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{\mathrm{init}}</annotation></semantics></math> is drawn from the Haar measure on <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> controls prior concentration. Low <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> yields a diffuse prior expressing ignorance about the adapter subspace, while high <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> anchors the posterior near the initialization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The SVD parameterization <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta W=U\Sigma V^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta W=U\Sigma V^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> is a deliberate design choice. Unlike the standard LoRA parameterization <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta W=BA" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta W=BA</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> are unconstrained, our factorization separates the geometric component (the orthonormal frames <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U,V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U,V</annotation></semantics></math> that determine the adapter subspace) from the scaling component (the singular values <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> that determine the magnitude of the update within that subspace). This separation is what enables us to place a geometry-aware prior on the subspace while using a simple Gaussian prior on the scale. The alternative of placing a Matrix Langevin prior directly on the product <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="BA" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">BA</annotation></semantics></math> would conflate subspace uncertainty with scale uncertainty, losing the interpretability and the calibration benefits that come from treating them separately.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We note that the number of adapter parameters in SBA is identical to standard LoRA: <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> has <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{out}}\times k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{out}}\times k</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> has <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{in}}\times k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{in}}\times k</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> has <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, for a total of <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(d_{\text{out}}+d_{\text{in}})\times k+k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(d_{\text{out}}+d_{\text{in}})\times k+k</annotation></semantics></math>. The orthonormality constraints reduce the effective degrees of freedom (the manifold dimension is <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dk-k(k+1)/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dk-k(k+1)/2</annotation></semantics></math> rather than <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dk" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dk</annotation></semantics></math>), but this is a feature, not a bug: the constraints encode the inductive bias that adapter subspaces should be well conditioned.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For classification with labels <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in\{1,\ldots,C\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in\{1,\ldots,C\}</annotation></semantics></math> and input features <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, the likelihood is <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid x,\{U^{(\ell)},\Sigma^{(\ell)},V^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell})=\mathrm{softmax}(f_{\theta}(x))_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid x,\{U^{(\ell)},\Sigma^{(\ell)},V^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell})=\mathrm{softmax}(f_{\theta}(x))_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the forward pass with adapted weights <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{0}^{(\ell)}+U^{(\ell)}\Sigma^{(\ell)}V^{(\ell)\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em">⊤</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{0}^{(\ell)}+U^{(\ell)}\Sigma^{(\ell)}V^{(\ell)\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Tangent Space Laplace Approximation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Exact posterior inference on the Stiefel manifold is intractable. We develop a tangent space Laplace approximation that exploits the manifold geometry while remaining computationally practical. The procedure has four steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We first find the MAP estimate <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{U}^{(\ell)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{U}^{(\ell)}</annotation></semantics></math> by optimizing the log-posterior using Riemannian SGD,</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{U}=\arg\max_{U\in\mathrm{St}(k,d)}\Big[\sum_{i}\log p(y_{i}\mid x_{i},U,\ldots)+\log p(U\mid F)\Big]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>U</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{U}=\arg\max_{U\in\mathrm{St}(k,d)}\Big[\sum_{i}\log p(y_{i}\mid x_{i},U,\ldots)+\log p(U\mid F)\Big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where the Riemannian gradient is obtained by projecting the Euclidean gradient onto <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{U}\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>U</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>St</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{U}\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> and applying the QR retraction. At the MAP estimate <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{U}</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute the Hessian of the log-posterior restricted to the tangent space <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\hat{U}}\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>St</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\hat{U}}\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>. Using an orthonormal basis <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{E_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{E_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\hat{U}}\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>St</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\hat{U}}\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> (where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=dk-k(k+1)/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=dk-k(k+1)/2</annotation></semantics></math>), we form the <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\times m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\times m</annotation></semantics></math> Hessian matrix <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{ij}=E_{i}^{\top}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{St}(k,d)}\log p(\hat{U}\mid\mathcal{D},F)\,E_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mo>∇</mo><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{ij}=E_{i}^{\top}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{St}(k,d)}\log p(\hat{U}\mid\mathcal{D},F)\,E_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>. For scalability, we use a KFAC approximation to <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, computed over a subset of the training data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The Laplace approximation in the tangent space is <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\xi)=\mathcal{N}(\xi\mid 0,(-H)^{-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\xi)=\mathcal{N}(\xi\mid 0,(-H)^{-1})</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi\in T_{\hat{U}}\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>St</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi\in T_{\hat{U}}\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>. To obtain posterior samples on <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>, we draw <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{U}^{(s)}\sim q(\xi_{U})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>ξ</mi><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>U</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{U}^{(s)}\sim q(\xi_{U})</annotation></semantics></math> and map back to the manifold via retraction, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{(s)}=\mathrm{Retr}_{\hat{U}}(\xi_{U}^{(s)})=\mathrm{qf}(\hat{U}+\xi_{U}^{(s)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Retr</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>ξ</mi><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>qf</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>ξ</mi><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{(s)}=\mathrm{Retr}_{\hat{U}}(\xi_{U}^{(s)})=\mathrm{qf}(\hat{U}+\xi_{U}^{(s)})</annotation></semantics></math>. Applying this sampling procedure symmetrically to all Bayesian parameters, the predictive distribution is then formed by averaging across samples:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y\mid x,\mathcal{D})\approx\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}p(y\mid x,U^{(s)},\Sigma^{(s)},V^{(s)})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>S</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>S</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y\mid x,\mathcal{D})\approx\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}p(y\mid x,U^{(s)},\Sigma^{(s)},V^{(s)}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17809v1/fig1_method_overview.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/150;" width="452" height="150"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Overview of Stiefel-Bayes Adapters. The Matrix Langevin prior respects the geometry of orthonormal adapter factors, and the tangent space Laplace approximation enables efficient posterior sampling via retraction.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Computational Considerations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The additional cost of SBA over deterministic orthogonal LoRA has three components: Riemannian gradient projection (one matrix multiplication per step, negligible), tangent space Hessian computation (a one-time post-training cost using KFAC over approximately 1000 data points, taking about 5 minutes on a single A100 for LLaMA-2-7B), and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> forward passes at inference for the predictive ensemble (Eq. <a href="#S3.E5" title="In 3.2 Tangent Space Laplace Approximation ‣ 3 Method: Stiefel-Bayes Adapters ‣ Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priorsfor Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). With <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=10</annotation></semantics></math> samples and KFAC Hessian, the total overhead is fewer than 8% wall-clock increase during training and roughly <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\times</annotation></semantics></math> inference cost. For selective prediction, even <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=5</annotation></semantics></math> samples suffice (Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 Ablation Studies ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priorsfor Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a>). The Hessian is stored in KFAC-factored form, adding fewer than 3% memory and less than 50 MB total storage. All <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> forward passes are independent and can be batched on a single GPU; in practice, batching <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=10</annotation></semantics></math> on a single A100 with LLaMA-2-7B requires approximately <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> the memory of a single forward pass. To further reduce inference cost, we explore predictive distillation in Section <a href="#S5.SS7" title="5.7 Predictive Distillation ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Calibrated Adaptation: Bayesian Stiefel Manifold Priorsfor Reliable Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Why Geometry Matters: Formal Analysis</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before presenting full experiments, we formalize why manifold-aware priors outperform flat-space alternatives. A common strategy to combine Bayesian inference with orthogonality is to define a Gaussian posterior <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(\hat{W},\Sigma_{A})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(\hat{W},\Sigma_{A})</annotation></semantics></math> over the ambient space <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}</annotation></semantics></math> and project it to <math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> via polar decomposition. We call this the projection problem: the induced distribution on <math id="S4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> concentrates in regions favored by the nonlinear projection map rather than by the data. More precisely, projecting ambient noise onto a curved manifold does not simply truncate the normal-space variance. Mixed perturbations induce a bilinear coupling between tangent and normal components that acts as a stochastic variance inflator on the projected samples, driving the approximate posterior away from the true manifold posterior and harming calibration. The following theorem captures this phenomenon formally.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Geometric Variance Inflation &amp; KL Tightness)<span id="Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{U}\in\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{U}\in\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> be the MAP estimate of the highly-concentrated target posterior <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathrm{post}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>post</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathrm{post}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathrm{tang}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>tang</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathrm{tang}}</annotation></semantics></math> be the intrinsic Laplace approximation, obtained by pushing forward <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{T})</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\hat{U}}\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>St</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\hat{U}}\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> through a second-order retraction <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> optimally matches the inverse Hessian of <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-\log p_{\mathrm{post}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>post</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\log p_{\mathrm{post}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathrm{proj}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>proj</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathrm{proj}}</annotation></semantics></math> be the ambient approximation, obtained by projecting an ambient Gaussian <math id="Thmtheorem1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(\hat{U},\Sigma_{A})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>U</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(\hat{U},\Sigma_{A})</annotation></semantics></math> onto <math id="Thmtheorem1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> via the polar projection <math id="Thmtheorem1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="Thmtheorem1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma_{A}=\Sigma_{T}\oplus\Sigma_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>⊕</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma_{A}=\Sigma_{T}\oplus\Sigma_{N}</annotation></semantics></math> decomposes orthogonally into tangent and normal covariances.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Then, under a local quadratic approximation of the posterior, the ambient normal noise strictly inflates the intrinsic variance, and the Kullback-Leibler divergences satisfy:</span></p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{KL}(q_{\mathrm{tang}}\|p_{\mathrm{post}})\leq\mathrm{KL}(q_{\mathrm{proj}}\|p_{\mathrm{post}})-\mathcal{E}(\Sigma_{T},\Sigma_{N})+O(\|\Sigma_{A}\|^{3/2})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>KL</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>tang</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>post</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>KL</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>proj</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>post</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{KL}(q_{\mathrm{tang}}\|p_{\mathrm{post}})\leq\mathrm{KL}(q_{\mathrm{proj}}\|p_{\mathrm{post}})-\mathcal{E}(\Sigma_{T},\Sigma_{N})+O(\|\Sigma_{A}\|^{3/2})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="Thmtheorem1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}(\Sigma_{T},\Sigma_{N})&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}(\Sigma_{T},\Sigma_{N})&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> is a strictly positive penalty governed by the normal variance.
